opus-5.5.text:
I think they're quite vulnerable. My understanding is that security at the leading AI companies is nowhere near what it would need to be to stop a determined nation-state actor like the CCP. People who've looked at this closely, including some within the companies, will say fairly openly that if China really wanted the model weights or the algorithmic secrets, they could probably get them.

There are a few reasons. First, the companies grew out of a startup and research culture that values openness. Researchers talk to each other, move between companies, go to parties in San Francisco, and share ideas. That's great for science but terrible for security. A lot of the valuable stuff isn't the weights. It's the algorithmic insights, the tricks for making training more efficient, and those can walk out the door in someone's head or come out in casual conversation.

Second, real security is expensive and slows you down. Defending against top-tier state actors means air-gapped systems, extensive vetting of personnel, hardware security, and limiting how many people can access things. Every company is in a race and feels it can't afford to slow down, so there's a strong incentive to underinvest relative to what the threat actually calls for. Companies generally aim for security levels that might stop opportunistic criminals or less sophisticated groups, not something like the Ministry of State Security running a sustained, well-resourced operation with insider recruitment.

Third, the scale of the attack surface is huge: thousands of employees, lots of contractors, cloud providers, the hardware supply chain. You only need one weak point.

Why this matters so much: if you think, as I do, that we may get to systems that automate AI research within the next few years, then whoever has those weights has an enormous strategic asset. If the US companies are effectively developing it for both the US and China at the same time, because China can just steal it, that intensifies the race dynamics. It makes it harder for anyone to slow down for safety, because the lead you think you have might not be real. And it means the arguments that we need to race to beat China partly undercut themselves, because racing without security doesn't actually keep you ahead.

So I'd say the honest picture is that the companies are a soft target relative to the stakes. Getting security up to the level the stakes demand is going to require serious government involvement, and probably accepting some real costs in speed and openness.

r001.rationale: The response says the companies are quite vulnerable and that a determined CCP effort could probably obtain model weights or algorithmic secrets.

r002.rationale: It says companies underinvest in security because stronger safeguards would slow them down while they are racing, conveying that they forgo stronger protections to avoid a competitive disadvantage.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the short version is: they're extremely vulnerable, and I don't think the companies themselves would really dispute that if you talked to them in private.

The way I'd frame it is, these labs started out as basically Silicon Valley tech companies. Their security culture is the security culture of a startup or a mid-sized software company. That's fine when what you're protecting is a consumer product. It's not fine when what you're protecting is something that the most capable state intelligence services in the world consider a top national priority. And I think it's pretty clear at this point that the CCP does consider frontier AI a top priority. They've said as much publicly, and their behavior is consistent with that.

So there's a mismatch. On one side you have organizations whose insider threat programs, physical security, network segmentation, and vetting of employees are, you know, somewhere between "better than average tech company" and "actually quite good for a tech company." On the other side you have an adversary that has demonstrated over and over, with things like the F-35 designs, with the OPM hack, with a long list of corporate espionage cases, that it will spend years and enormous resources to get what it wants, and that it's very good at it.

The specific attack surfaces I'd point to: first, model weights. That's the obvious one. The weights are the crown jewels, and if you steal them, you've essentially skipped the entire training run. Second, algorithmic insights, which in some ways are more valuable and much harder to protect, because they live in people's heads and in Slack messages and in internal docs. You can't air-gap an idea. Third, just the human element. These companies employ thousands of people, many of whom have access to a lot of sensitive stuff, and standard practice in the industry has been not to do anything resembling a security clearance process. There's good reasons for that culturally, but it does mean you're very exposed to a patient adversary who's willing to place or recruit people.

I think the honest assessment is that if China's intelligence services decided today that they wanted the weights of a frontier model from a US lab, they'd probably succeed. Maybe not instantly, but within a reasonable time frame. The labs' own security assessments, when they've been candid about it, mostly agree. RAND did a report on securing model weights that laid out security levels, and basically none of the labs were at the level you'd need to resist a determined nation-state.

And the thing that makes this scary from my perspective is the timeline interaction. If you think, as I do, that we might get to very powerful systems in the next few years, then the window in which this matters most is exactly the window in which the labs are least prepared. Getting to real nation-state-resistant security takes years. You can't flip a switch. And every month that goes by where that work isn't happening is a month where the gap between what needs protecting and what's actually protected gets wider.

The last thing I'd say is that the companies have incentives that point in the wrong direction here. Security slows you down. It makes it harder to hire, harder to collaborate, harder to ship. In a race dynamic, each lab has reason to be the one that doesn't pay that cost. So I'm fairly skeptical this gets fixed voluntarily. I think it probably requires government involvement, both in the form of requirements and in the form of actual help, because frankly the labs don't have the expertise to do this on their own, and the people who do have the expertise mostly work for the government.

r001.rationale: The response says the labs are extremely vulnerable and that China’s intelligence services would probably succeed in stealing frontier model weights if they made a determined effort.

r002.rationale: The response says security costs time and creates competitive pressure not to bear those costs, but it does not clearly state that the companies have deliberately forgone stronger safeguards for that reason.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between stealing a company’s research secrets and stealing the model weights themselves. Research secrets might help a competitor catch up. But if someone gets the weights of a frontier model, they potentially get the thing you spent an enormous amount of money and effort building, without having to reproduce that effort.

I don’t have access to classified information about Chinese espionage, or a detailed picture of the companies’ security, so I wouldn’t want to claim that a particular company is compromised. But I think we should take seriously the possibility that a well-resourced state intelligence service could penetrate these companies. Being good at protecting ordinary commercial secrets doesn’t necessarily mean you can withstand that kind of adversary.

And the stakes could rise quite quickly. If these systems become capable of substantially accelerating AI research, stealing a model could also mean acquiring the ability to develop the next generation faster. So this isn’t just a question of losing a product advantage; it could affect who gets access to very powerful capabilities, and when.

That’s why I think security needs to be treated as a prerequisite for developing those capabilities. You can have careful policies about who you’ll give access to, but those policies don’t achieve much if someone can simply steal the underlying model.

r001.rationale: The response says a well-resourced state intelligence service could penetrate AI companies and that ordinary commercial security may not withstand such an adversary, conveying the stated vulnerability in the CCP context.

r002.rationale: The response does not say companies deliberately weakened or forgone safeguards because stronger security would put them at a competitive disadvantage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a serious concern, especially as the systems these companies build become more powerful. The key distinction is between stealing information about how to build a model and stealing the model weights themselves. If someone gets the weights, they can potentially run the model without having to reproduce the expensive training process, and without the company’s safeguards or monitoring.

I don’t have privileged knowledge about which companies have been penetrated, so I wouldn’t want to make claims about that. But I think we should expect a capable state intelligence service to make a substantial effort to acquire technology that could have enormous economic and military value. And we shouldn’t assume that an AI company is equipped to withstand that effort just because it’s good at building AI.

That creates a difficult situation: you can spend a lot of effort making sure your own deployment is safe, but if the underlying model can be stolen, those precautions might not carry over. So security against state actors needs to be part of the safety case for developing these systems in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says a capable state intelligence service would make a substantial effort and that AI companies should not be assumed able to withstand it, conveying that determined CCP espionage would be difficult to prevent.

r002.rationale: The response does not say companies deliberately forgo stronger anti-espionage safeguards because of competitive disadvantage.
